2531: Grief is a normal human response to the loss of a significant person. It involves adapting to a new reality and learning to live in a world where the person who has died is no longer present.
2533: It is influenced by factors such as the relationship with the person who died, the circumstances of the death, life history and the support network available. It can show up through different reactions, especially in the early stages.
2538: A feeling of helplessness or emptiness
2539: Tightness in the chest or throat
2543: A feeling of emptiness in the stomach
2546: Persistent thoughts about the person who has died
2547: A sense of presence or transient auditory/visual experiences related to the person who has died
2551: Looking for objects or memories associated with the person
2553: Accepting the reality of the loss
2556: Preserving a symbolic bond with the person who has gone, bringing their presence into memory and affection while carrying on living
2557: The intervention should focus on active listening, emotional validation and support for gradual adaptation to the loss.
2558: Facilitate acceptance of the loss: Allow the person to talk about the death, the funeral or the circumstances of the loss, helping to integrate the reality of what has happened.
2559: Help with identifying emotions: Encourage the expression of difficult emotions, such as guilt, anger or sadness, without judgement.
2560: Support the reorganisation of daily life: Help with adapting to new responsibilities, decisions or routines.
2561: Use symbolic elements: Photographs, letters, rituals or memories can facilitate emotional expression and meaningful connection.
2562: Validate the legacy of the person who has died: Promote ways of honouring the story and meaning of the person who has been lost.
2563: Using clichés or minimising the pain: Avoid phrases such as “You have to be strong”, “Time heals everything”, “I know exactly how you feel”.
2564: Expecting rigid stages: Grief does not follow a linear sequence or the same one for everyone.
2565: Encouraging impulsive decisions: Avoid major life changes immediately after the loss.
2566: Pathologising initial reactions: Intense crying, frequent dreams or a sense of the deceased’s presence can be part of the normal grieving process.
2567: Assuming everyone needs therapy: Many people adapt with informal support and relational support.
2568: Referral to psychological support should be considered when:
2569: !The distress remains intense and persistent for a long period
2570: !There is a significant inability to resume personal, social or professional functioning
2571: !Severe symptoms of anxiety, depression or substance abuse appear
2572: !The person remains “stuck” in the loss, unable to integrate the absence
2573: !There are persistent physical symptoms with no medical explanation
2574: !There are self-harming behaviours, suicidal ideation or risk behaviours

2581: A panic attack is a sudden episode of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within a few minutes. Although the symptoms can be very frightening, a panic attack is not dangerous and corresponds to an intense activation of the body’s alarm system.
2583: The body goes into “fight or flight”
2584: During a panic attack, the body goes into a state of “fight or flight”, intensely activating the sympathetic nervous system.
2587: A feeling of breathlessness or choking
2595: Fear of going mad or dying
2596: A feeling of strangeness or unreality (derealisation)
2597: A feeling of being “outside the body” (depersonalisation)
2599: The panic cycle and anticipatory anxiety
2601: They are interpreted as signs of serious danger“I’m going to die”, “I’m having a heart attack”, “I’m going mad”
2602: The sense of threat increasesThe body becomes even more activated and the physical symptoms intensify.
2603: And the cycle starts again: a panic cycle is created.
2605: After a panic attack, a persistent fear of experiencing the symptoms again may appear.
2606: “What if it happens again?”, “What if I faint in front of everyone?”
2607: This can increase bodily hypervigilance and avoidance behaviours.
2608: The priority is to help the person feel safe and gradually regulate their nervous system.
2609: Normalise and validate: Explain that the symptoms are an intense anxiety response and that they will ease with time.
2610: Help with breathing: Use slow, diaphragmatic breathing to reduce hyperventilation and physical tension.
2611: Promote grounding: Help the person focus on the present moment through the senses: identify objects around them, listen to sounds, feel their feet on the floor.
2612: Encourage compassionate self-talk: Encourage phrases such as “this is anxiety”, “I’ve been through this before”, “the symptoms will pass”.
2613: Reduce the sense of danger: Speak in a calm, simple and predictable way.
2614: Stay in place, if possible: Avoiding an immediate escape from the situation can help the brain relearn that the context is safe.
2615: Minimising or ridiculing: Avoid phrases such as “Calm down, it’s nothing”, “You’re exaggerating”.
2616: Feeding catastrophic interpretations: Do not reinforce the idea that the person is in imminent danger without a medical assessment.
2617: Pressing them to “get a grip”: Trying to force calm quickly can increase anxiety and shame.
2618: Encouraging excessive avoidance: Leaving all situations associated with panic immediately can reinforce future fear.
2619: Fighting the anxiety: Trying to eliminate the symptoms completely or “not think about it” tends to increase focus and distress.
2620: Referral for medical and/or psychological assessment should be considered when:
2621: !It is the first episode of panic
2622: !There are doubts about a medical cause for the symptoms
2623: !The attacks become frequent or persistent
2624: !There is a significant impact on work or daily life
2625: !The person starts avoiding meetings, presentations or places for fear of another attack
2626: !Constant anticipatory anxiety appears
2627: !Alcohol, sedatives or other substances are being used to cope with the symptoms
2628: !Regulation strategies are no longer enough

2632: Some situations call for a more immediate response. A panic attack gives no warning – it happens suddenly and can be very frightening for the person experiencing it and for those next to them. The role of the person offering support is not to diagnose or solve, but to create safety and help the person regulate.
